post.description:
`Download`, not `Manage`: a restore is the first half of taking a copy, and somebody who may download an
asset may ask for its bytes to be fetchable. It is also where the cost sits, which is why the threshold
exists — the answer to an expensive request is "somebody senior confirms", not "no".

parameters.name: tier
parameters.description:

parameters.description: How long the copy stays warm. Defaults to seven days (§6.5).

get.summary: What each tier would cost and when it would land, without asking for anything.
get.description:
§6.5 requires the estimate *before* the user confirms, and without this endpoint there was no way to
honour that: the only thing that produced a plan was the POST, which also records the request. So a screen
could either show a price or ask for a restore, and showing the price meant having already asked.

All three tiers in one response rather than one call per tier. The whole reason to show a number is the
comparison — 10× on price against 100× on latency — and three round trips to assemble one table would
leave a screen rendering half a decision.

A tier the class cannot offer is present with `available: false` and the reason, rather than absent. Deep
Archive has no Expedited, and a chooser that silently showed two options where another asset shows three
invites "why is this one different" — which is a question the response can simply answer.

grant. It inherits the order's expiry, so the window an approver granted is the window the link has.

post.summary: Turns a question into a query.
post.description:
## Why this returns a query rather than results

Because the answer belongs in the search box. Somebody can see what was understood, correct it, and keep it —
and the results then come from the ordinary search path, under the ordinary predicate, with no second code
path that could filter differently. A model that answered with *assets* would be a second retrieval route
into a governed library, which is exactly what §12 argues against.

## Read, and paid

Searching is what a reader does, so gating this behind Manage would put it where it is not needed. It costs a
call per question, which is why it has its own switch (`enrichment_settings.natural_language_search`, off by
default) and why the AI spend cap applies. The cap is the control.

200.description: The translation; check `parses` before using it

422.description: Natural-language search is off, there is no credential, or the question is empty

429.description: The tenant is over its hard AI spend cap for this month

get.summary: The caller's current search as a CSV (Q.18).
get.description:
**Answered in SQL, always, even for a query the index would rank.** An export is a *set*, not a ranking: it
is a file somebody re-imports, audits, or hands to a client, and the two failure modes of the ranked path
are both silent omission. The index is eventually consistent, so an asset edited a moment ago may not be in
it; and the ranked path's total is capped by the overfetch depth, so a large set cannot even be measured
there — which is how the first version of this endpoint came to export nothing at all from an index that had
never been built.

The cost is stated rather than hidden: for a free-text query, SQL matches substrings where the index matches
tokens, so a text export can differ slightly from the ranked grid it was taken from. Every structured query
— a field, a facet click, a category, a filename — is identical in both. Completeness is the property an
export needs, and a file that quietly omits rows is worse than one that includes a near-miss.

Read scope. An export of metadata somebody can already read is not a disclosure — see `orders::metadata_csv`
on why the same file is not offered to an unauthenticated recipient.

post.summary: Consumes one download from an order pickup, for one named item.
post.description:
The asset id is in the path and checked against the order's items — a pickup is an agreement about a specific
set, and letting a recipient name any id would turn one approval into a key to the library.

The download lands in the usage ledger (Q.12) as a *declared* use, attributed to the person who asked for the
order. They named the channel and territory when they placed it and an approver agreed to it, which is a
stronger record than most downloads carry. The recipient collecting has no identity here, so recording them is
not an option; recording the requester is the honest answer to "who is accountable for this copy".

oneOf.description: Who did it. Absent for something the system did, and for somebody since deleted.

`upload`, `edit`, `share`, `comment`, `download`, `delete`, `restore` — or anything a future subsystem
records. Reported as stored rather than mapped onto a known set, so activity this build does not recognise
is still visible.

new_asset_id.description: An asset this caller uploaded through the ordinary route. See the module docs on why it is not a file.

out_of_scope.description:
Ids the caller cannot see, counted rather than named.

Counted because naming them would confirm they exist, which is the existence oracle the asset rule
exists to close. Reported at all because "I selected forty and got thirty-eight" needs an answer.

AmendBody.description: What may be changed. Not the key.

AmendCommentRequest.description: What to change about a comment. One of the two, never both — see the module docs.

AmendMappingRequest.description: What to change. An omitted member is left alone.

AmendProfileRequest.description: What to change. An omitted member is left alone.

AmendRequest.description: What to change. An omitted member is left alone; `search_alias: null` clears it.

search_alias.description:
Doubly optional: absent leaves the alias alone, `null` removes it. Those are different intents and
a single `Option` cannot express both.

AmendTypeRequest.description:
What to change about a type. An omitted member is left alone.

`field_keys` replaces the list wholesale rather than merging: a type's fields are an ordered list, and
"add this one" computed against a client's stale copy would silently drop whatever it had not seen.

assets_now_incomplete.description: How many live assets would now fail a metadata write for want of a newly-required value.

reindex_required.description: Whether the search index is now stale and needs rebuilding.

AmendedField.description: An amended field, with the consequences of the amendment.

question.description: What somebody typed. "Harbour photos from last week", not a query.

AskResult.description: What the model made of it.

confidence.description: As claimed by the model. Shown, never used as a gate.

explanation.description: One sentence for the person who asked, so a wrong query is correctable rather than mysterious.

parses.description:
Whether the query parses. **A caller must check this**: a query that does not parse is not a query, and
the honest fallback is to search the question as plain text — which is what the box would have done for
free.

oneOf.description: Why it does not parse, when it does not: the parser's own message and column.

shorthand.description: The query, in the same syntax a person types. Put it in the search box and search.

content_hash.description: BLAKE3 of the original bytes, lowercase hex. What deduplication and integrity both key on.

engagement.description:
Ratings, favourites and the watch state, in full (Q.5b·3).

The whole picture here, unlike the two fields the summary carries: the panel draws the star widget, the
counts and the watch toggle, and fetching them separately would make opening a panel two requests where
one will do.

legal_hold.description:
Blocks tiering *and* deletion. Surfaced because a user who cannot delete an asset deserves to know
why rather than to see a failing button.

preview_url.description:
A signed internal-preview URL for the `preview-1024` rendition, when one has been rendered.

On the detail endpoint only. A list of sixty of these would mint sixty tokens for images no grid draws —
the grid uses the thumbnail — and a lightbox opens one asset at a time.

`Contain`-fitted rather than cropped, which is what makes it the right image for somebody inspecting an
asset: the thumbnail is a 256px square crop, so enlarging it is a blurry crop of the wrong aspect.

technical.description:
Probed technical facts — EXIF, codec, colour. Read-only, and shaped by the file rather than by the
tenant's schema, so it is not merged into `values`.

values.description: The validated metadata, keyed by field definition key.

AssetDetail.description: One asset in full, as the detail panel draws it.

AssetPage.description:
One page of results.

`total` is separate from `items.len()` and load-bearing for accessibility: a virtualised grid must
report the real row count in `aria-rowcount`, or a screen reader announces "20 items" for a library
of a hundred thousand.

did_you_mean.description:
A query worth trying instead, when this one matched nothing (Q.17).

Only ever set on an empty result set, and only when a value close to one the caller typed really exists
in their visible library — so it is an offer to run something that will work, not a guess. Absent
otherwise, including when the search simply has no matches: "no results" with no suggestion is an
honest answer, and inventing one would send somebody round a second empty loop.

offset.description: Zero-based index of the first item in `items` within the full result set.

ranked.description:
Whether `items` are in relevance order.

False when the query contained a clause the index cannot answer — category or collection membership,
which are joins — so it was answered in SQL and ordered by recency instead. Reported rather than left
implicit because a grid that says "ranked by relevance" over a `created_at` ordering is lying about the
one thing a reader might act on; and because the *count* means something different too, being exact
rather than capped by the ranking overfetch.

total.description: Total matching assets, not the number returned.

AssetSummary.description:
One asset, as the grid renders it.

Deliberately small. A 100k-row grid fetches pages of these, so every field here is multiplied by
the page size — and anything a cell does not draw belongs on the detail endpoint instead.

average_stars.description:
The asset's average rating, or `None` when nobody has rated it.

The average rather than the caller's own rating: a grid shows what the library thinks, and `None` is not
zero — "unrated" and "rated badly by everyone" must not draw the same.

filename.description: The name the uploader gave it, preserved verbatim. The stored MIME is sniffed, not this.

has_attachment.description:
Whether it has paperwork attached (Q.9) — a release, a licence.

A boolean rather than a count, because the question a cell answers is "is the rights picture documented",
and *how many* documents there are is a detail for the panel. Scoped like everything else: paperwork the
caller cannot see does not count, or the flag would disclose that something exists.

is_favourite.description:
Whether *this caller* has favourited it, so a cell can draw a filled star (Q.5b·3).

Only the two engagement facts a cell actually draws are here — see the note on this struct about every
field being multiplied by the page size. The counts, the caller's own stars and the watch state are on the
detail endpoint, because no grid cell shows them.

mime.description: Sniffed on ingest, never taken from the client (`assets.mime`).

published_at.description:
When somebody published this asset, or absent (Q.14).

Publication is a per-asset act, and it is what a live-query portal rests on. On a grid it is a chip:
the difference between "in the library" and "on a public page" is the one a person needs to see before
they act on a selection.

rights_state.description:
Rights evaluation outcome. A *display* input: enforcement happens at the distribution
chokepoint (D12), and this field is what dims a button rather than what protects an asset.

tag_confidence.description:
Model confidence in the asset's automatic tags, 0..1. `None` means nothing scored it — which
is not the same as zero, and the UI renders it differently.

thumbnail_url.description:
URL of the thumbnail, as a signed internal-preview delivery URL.

Absolute when the deployment configures `server.public_url`, root-relative otherwise — so a client on a
different origin must resolve it against the API's base rather than its own. Absent when the asset has
no thumbnail yet, which is the normal state between an upload finishing and the worker deriving it: a
URL minted regardless would 404, and a grid cannot tell a broken link from work still in progress.

tier.description:
Where the original lives, derived server-side from storage class and restore state so the UI
never reimplements that mapping.

width.description:
Display dimensions — orientation already applied, so a grid cell can lay out from these
without knowing about EXIF. `None` for formats with no intrinsic size.

AssetTier.description:
The tier a user sees.

Derived from two independent columns — the object's storage class and the state of any restore —
and derived **here** rather than in the UI, because the mapping contains a trap: a restore does not
change an object's storage class, so an *expired* restore of an archived object is archived again.
The schema says so twice, and reimplementing the rule in TypeScript is how a download button stays
enabled until the day someone presses it.

AssetTypeView.description: Which type an asset has, and the form that follows from it.

field_keys.description:
The fields that apply *now*, in order — the resolved answer rather than the stored pointer, because
this is what the client has to draw.

metadata_type_id.description:
`None` means the asset falls back — to the tenant's default type, or to the whole vocabulary when
there is no default. Either way it still has a form; see `dam_db::metadata_types`.

AttachRequest.description: Which already-uploaded asset to attach, and as what.

outstanding.description: How many assets are waiting to be described, at the moment it was queued.

BackfillRequest.description: Starts, or nudges, a library-wide description.

slice.description:
How many assets per batch. Smaller slices land their first descriptions sooner; the default is what the
pipeline picks.

BackfillView.description: How a library-wide description is getting on.

in_flight.description: Requests sitting in a batch that has not ended yet.

outstanding.description: Assets with a proxy that no model has described under the current prompt.

running.description: Whether a slice is queued or in flight right now.

id.description:
A stable identifier where one exists — a taxonomy term id. Absent for a metadata value, whose identity
*is* its text.

value.description:
The value as text. A number or a boolean is rendered rather than typed, because a rail displays it and
the round trip back into a query goes through the field's kind anyway.

hard.description: `true` to refuse enrichment past the limit rather than only warning.

warn_at_fraction.description: Where the warning fires. 0.8 gives a customer time to react rather than discovering the cap by hitting it.

BudgetView.description: The cap, and what has been spent against it.

enforcement.description: `soft` warns and keeps working; `hard` refuses new enrichment.

limit_cents.description: `null` when no cap is configured, which is not a cap of zero — enrichment runs unmetered.

period_start.description: The first day of the calendar month the spend is counted in, in UTC.

state.description: What state the tenant is in right now: `allowed`, `warned` or `refused`.

BulkFailure.description: One failed row, for the report.

out_of_scope.description:
How many of the submitted ids fell out of scope. Reported as a count and nothing more: which ones,
and whether they exist at all, is exactly what §7 says a caller must not learn.

sample.description: A sample of the targets, for a dialog to name a few rather than list thousands.

target_count.description:
How many assets the operation would touch — after the caller's own scope is applied, so it is the
number that will actually be touched.

asset_ids.description: The selection. Deduplicated server-side; ids the caller may not manage fall out silently.

params.description:
Kind-specific parameters — for `metadata_set`, `{ "values": { … } }` with the same patch semantics
as the single-asset endpoint: `null` clears, absent leaves alone.

BulkStatus.description: An operation as the UI polls it.

failures.description: The first failures, row by row — "must report exactly which rows did not apply".

terminal.description: Whether the state is final, so a client polls this instead of re-implementing the state vocabulary.

key.description: Stable, and not changeable. A portal references this.

pin_hot.description: Whether membership blocks tiering (§6.4). A pinned collection's assets stay instantly fetchable.

CommentView.description: One comment, as a thread draws it.

edited_at.description:
Set when the words changed after posting, so a thread can say "edited" rather than silently showing
different text than whoever replied to it read.

parent_id.description: The comment this replies to, if any. Threads are one level deep.

recipients.description: Who this was addressed to. Routing — and, on a private comment, also who may read it.

oneOf.description: Who last moved the status. Absent while it is still as posted.

visibility.description: `public` or `private`. A private comment reaches its author and its recipients, and nobody else.

ConversionRequest.description: A conversion to create or redefine.

key.description:
Required on create, ignored on redefine — a delivery token carries the key, so renaming one would
strand links that were valid when they were sent.

ConversionView.description: One named format, as a person choosing sees it.

description.description: Written for whoever is choosing. The reason this table exists rather than a list of sizes.

key.description: The name a download request carries. Stable across relabelling.

required_permission.description:
The permission a role must carry. Present for administration; the download options never list a format
the caller cannot use, so it is always `null` there.

Counts.description: The counts a landing page leads with.

without_metadata.description: Assets carrying no metadata at all — the work a landing page exists to surface.

enabled.description: Defaults to true: a mapping saved and then not applied would be a surprising thing to have to switch on.

overwrite.description: Defaults to false, which is the safe direction: see the note in `dam_db::auto_import`.

CreateNodeRequest.description: A category to create within a tree.

ai_tags_enabled.description:
Defaults to true: tagging on is the ordinary case, and a profile that silently disabled enrichment
would be a surprising default to inherit.

public_url.description:
The public URL, when the portal is public. `null` otherwise, rather than a URL that would 404 — a link
that does not work is worse than no link.

url.description: The token URL, readable exactly once: the token is stored as a digest, so this response is the only copy.

CreatedShare.description: A created share. The token appears here and nowhere else, exactly like an issued API key.

portal_path.description: The path a recipient opens, for the client to compose onto its own origin.

token.description:
The one-time token. The table holds a digest, so a lost link cannot be recovered — revoke and
re-create, which is the same posture as an API key and for the same reason.

CredentialActiveRequest.description:
Whether a credential is withdrawn or in use.

Named for the credential rather than reusing `conversions::ActiveRequest`: utoipa keys components by type
name, and two `ActiveRequest`s in one document would silently be one schema.

CredentialView.description: One credential, as an administrator sees it. No key, sealed or otherwise.

base_url.description: `null` for Anthropic's own endpoint. Required for everything else.

hint.description:
The last four characters of the key. Enough to recognise which of two keys a row holds, useless to
anybody who steals the response.

needs_resealing.description:
Whether this row is still sealed under a retired key.

The rotation worklist, computed without opening anything. An operator who has rotated the sealing key
needs to know which credentials still need re-sealing, and the answer must not require decrypting them
to find out.

provider.description:
`anthropic` or `openai_compatible` — the wire format, not the vendor. See
`dam_db::ai_credentials::Provider`.

spotlights.description: Saved searches this caller may open, theirs first.

note.description: Why it was refused, or a condition on an approval.

DefineRequest.description: A field to define. Flags default to the conservative reading when omitted.

searchable.description: Defaults to true: a field nobody can search for is the surprising choice, not the safe one.

DownloadIssued.description: A URL to fetch, or word that the format is being made.

format.description: What was asked for, echoed so a client holding several requests can tell them apart.

restore_url.description:
Where to ask for a restore, on `archived`. Absent otherwise.

Present because a URL that will 202 is worse than no URL: the client has something that looks
fetchable, hands it to a browser, and the wait shows up as a mystery in somebody else's response. The
mint knows the bytes are cold, so it says so here rather than letting the delivery route say it later.

status.description:
`ready`, `rendering`, or `archived`. A client polls on `rendering` and asks for a restore on
`archived`.

url.description: The signed URL. Absent while a conversion is still being rendered.

DownloadOptions.description: What one asset can be had as.

conversions.description:
The formats this caller may ask for, in the order somebody configured. See `original_available` on what
this list does and does not promise.

media_class.description:
The asset's media class, so a client can say "no formats are configured for video yet" rather than
showing an empty list with no explanation.

original_available.description:
Whether the untransformed bytes can be fetched now.

False for archived bytes and for a restore in flight: offering them would be offering a download that
begins a wait nobody was told about.

It says nothing about the conversions below it. A conversion that has *already* been rendered is its own
object and does not tier, so it stays available while the original does not — but one that has not been
rendered is produced from the original (`derive::asset` reads the original bytes), so for an archived
asset it needs the same restore. This response does not yet distinguish those two cases: the readiness
of a particular format is the download route's answer, and that route does not exist yet. Listing a
format here means the tenant offers it, not that its bytes exist this second.

DownloadRequest.description: What to download, and what for.

channel.description:
Where the copy is going, which is what rights are evaluated against.

Optional, and its *presence* is the declaration: a request that names a channel is one where somebody
answered, and the ledger row says so. Absent, the API supplies the narrowest honest default — a generic
internal channel — and records that nobody was asked. See migration 0024 on why the difference is worth
a column.

Not required outright, because a machine integration genuinely has one fixed usage and making it restate
it on every call would be ceremony. What must not happen is a default that *looks* like an answer.

format.description:
`original`, or a conversion's key. Defaults to the original, because that is what "download" means
without further information.

EngagementView.description:
An asset's engagement, as the caller may see it.

`Deserialize` as well as `Serialize` because `AssetDetail` embeds it and that type round-trips in the tests
and in the generated client; `PartialEq` for the same reason.

average_stars.description:
The mean of every rating, or null when nobody has rated it.

Null rather than zero: "unrated" and "rated badly by everyone" are different facts, and a widget that
drew them the same way would be lying about one of them.

my_stars.description: This caller's own rating. Never anybody else's.

EnrichmentSettings.description: What a model should do for this tenant.

alt_text_field.description: Where the alt text lands. `null` writes none.

guidance.description: The tenant's own instructions, and the cacheable half of every request.

is_enabled.description: False until somebody turns it on. This is the pipeline that bills per asset.

model.description: Overrides the credential's default model for this pipeline.

natural_language_search.description:
Whether a question in the search box may be turned into a query by a model.

Its own switch, not part of `is_enabled`: describing the library costs per asset and answering questions
costs per question, and a tenant may want either alone. Adding a key to describe a library should not
silently make every reader's search box a paid endpoint.

Facet.description: One facetable field and its buckets.

truncated.description: Whether buckets were dropped by the limit. Reported rather than left implicit — see [`FACET_BUCKETS`].

FieldDefinition.description: One field definition, as a form needs it.

ai_writable.description: Whether an enrichment run may write it.

oneOf.description:
When this field applies at all (Q.19b).

Present so the editor can *hide* an inapplicable field rather than offering one whose value the server
will refuse. The refusal exists too — a client is not trusted with a rule — but a form that asks a
question and then rejects the answer is a form nobody trusts back.

kind.description: The database spelling of the kind, so a client can pick an input type.

label.description: The tenant's own label. A form shows this rather than the key.

multivalued.description:
Whether the field takes an array.

Load-bearing rather than informational: a client that does not know this sends a comma-joined string
to a field that takes an array, and the server refuses it with a message about delimiters that the
user cannot act on. Discovered exactly that way, editing a multivalued field in a real browser.

read_only.description: Set by ingest or by a connector; an editor must not offer it.

search_alias.description: The shorthand prefix, when the tenant defined one: `bra:acme` for `brand`.

FieldDependency.description: The condition a dependent field hangs off (Q.19b).

values.description: The values that make this one apply. Compared as text, so `true` and `2026` work as written.

ItemView.description:
A collection's members, in their curated order.

Only the ones this caller can see. Reading membership is the mirror of [`add`]: if a scoped curator
listed a collection curated by somebody with a wider scope, the ids and the count would tell them about
assets they cannot read — the same existence oracle, arrived at from the other side. The positions are
the real ones, so a gap in the numbering is the honest signal that the collection holds more than this.

thumbnail_url.description:
A short-lived preview link, present only when the asset has a thumbnail derivative *and* delivery is
configured. Curation is visual: reordering a set of photographs by filename is a different and much
worse job than reordering it by looking at them.

LatencyClass.description:
How long a `GET` takes to become possible.

The download path and the UI branch on **this**, not on the provider name. That is
what lets Azure Archive or LTO tape slot in later without special-casing (§6.1).

ListPage.description:
A page of the caller's own favourites or watches.

Whole assets, not ids. Ids were the first shape here, on the reasoning that a grid already knows how to render
a set of assets — but there is no endpoint that fetches assets *by id set*, so a client holding fifty ids had
fifty requests to make. Returning the same `AssetPage` the browse and search endpoints return means one
request and one renderer, which is what the ids were supposed to achieve.

items.description:
Ordered by when *this caller* added each one, newest first — which is the order that makes a private list
legible, and is not the order any other endpoint can produce.

offset.description: Zero-based index of the first item within the full list.

total.description: How many the caller has *and can still see* — the same predicate the page came from.

MachineFieldView.description: A machine-written value, as the disclosure surface shows it (G2).

model.description: The model that produced it, as it answered.

MappingRow.description: A mapping as a client sees it.

overwrite.description: Whether this mapping may replace a value the asset already has.

priority.description: Lower fires first when several sources feed one field.

source.description: The embedded name, as the extractor reports it — `exif.artist`, `xmp.creator`.

MetadataAccepted.description: The outcome of a metadata edit.

values.description:
The stored document after the merge, so a client does not have to guess what the validator
normalised — a date reformatted or a number coerced would otherwise show up as an unexplained diff
on the next read.

MetadataPatch.description: A metadata edit: the fields to change, keyed by definition key.

values.description:
A merge, not a replacement. `null` for a value clears that field; a key that is absent is left
alone. Two clients editing different fields of one asset must not overwrite each other, and a PUT of
the whole document guarantees they do.

MetadataTypeRow.description: A metadata type, with the count that decides whether editing it is safe.

applies_to.description: The media classes this type is the natural choice for at ingest.

assets.description:
How many live assets currently carry this type.

On the row for the same reason a field's usage count is: removing a type re-forms every asset that
referenced it, and an administrator should not have to go and ask how many that is.

field_keys.description: Its fields, in its own order.

key.description: The stable name a portal will reference. Lowercase, and it cannot be changed later.

visibility.description:
Defaults to `private`, which is the safe direction: a collection that became public because somebody
omitted a field is a disclosure caused by a default.

NewCredentialRequest.description: A credential to store. The only shape in this API that carries a plaintext key.

api_key.description: The provider's key. Sealed before the response is written and never readable again.

base_url.description:
Required for `openai_compatible`, including the version segment —
`https://api.moonshot.ai/v1`, `https://api.groq.com/openai/v1`. Optional for Anthropic, where it
overrides the vendor endpoint with a gateway.

default_model.description: The model to use when a pipeline stage does not name one.

label.description: What to call it in a list. A person's name for the key, not the vendor's.

make_default.description: Whether enrichment should use this one.

collection_id.description: The collection whose members the portal shows.

is_public.description: Whether the slug resolves. False means the portal is reachable only by its token.

key.description: The URL name: lower-case letters, digits and hyphens.

media_class.description: A media class ("every video") as the source. Refused for the same reason.

passcode.description: The access half, handed straight to the share machinery.

saved_search_id.description:
A saved search as the source. Accepted by the schema, refused by this build — see the module note and
NEEDS-REVIEW.md. Named in the request rather than absent from it, so asking gets an answer about the
decision instead of "missing field `collection_id`".

NodeRow.description: One node, with the count of assets the caller can see at or beneath it.

assets.description: Distinct assets **this caller** can see in this category or any beneath it.

depth.description: Depth, so a client indents without parsing `path`.

path.description:
The ltree path. Exposed because the descendant filter uses it, and a client linking to a subtree
should not need another round trip to learn it.

filename.description: The name as asked for, so an order reads sensibly after a rename or a deletion.

OrderRequest.description: The complete field order, in the order fields should appear.

expired.description:
Whether the pickup window has closed. Derived from `expires_at` rather than stored — a stored `expired`
would need a sweeper to stay true and would be wrong between sweeps.

pickup_url.description:
The pickup URL, **only** on the response that just minted it.

A share token is stored as a digest, so it cannot be shown again — the same property that makes a leaked
database not a leaked set of links. Anybody who needs the link again re-issues the pickup, which revokes
the previous one; see [`fulfil`]. Absent on every ordinary read, which is why it is optional rather than a
separate response type.

self_approved.description: Whether the requester decided their own order. Reported rather than prevented — see the db module.

PersonView.description: A person, as a thread names them.

email.description:
Included because two colleagues can share a display name, and a picker that cannot tell them apart
misroutes a private comment — the one failure this list exists to prevent.

name.description: The name to show, falling back to the email when nobody set one.

asset_ids.description: The assets asked for. Narrowed to what this caller may see; see the db module on why silently.

channel.description: The intended use (Q.12), carried into the ledger when the pickup is collected.

conversion_key.description: Which named format (Q.11). Absent means the original.

purpose.description: Why. The entire question an approver answers, so it is required.

recipients.description: Who the delivery is for. Plural because an order is usually for a team.

PlacementState.description:
Lifecycle state of one `object_placements` row.

Mirrors the `object_placements.state` CHECK. In `dam-core` rather than `dam-store`
because both the database layer that loads it and the resolution layer that acts on it
need the same vocabulary — and a second definition is how the two drift.

Only `Present` is readable. The others each mean something different to an operator,
which is why this is not a boolean: `Uploading` will resolve itself, `Missing` needs a
re-replication, `Corrupt` needs a scrub, and `Deleting` is expected to disappear.

PlanView.description: What one policy would do, without doing it.

dry_run.description: Whether executing this policy would move anything at all.

halted.description:
Present when the run stopped early, with what stopped it. A truncated plan that did not say so reads
exactly like a policy that is working.

skipped.description: Every candidate that was examined and left alone, with why. The answer to "why did nothing happen?".

PolicyView.description: One tiering rule, as an administrator reads it.

after_days.description: Days of idleness before an object is eligible.

dry_run.description:
**True by default.** A policy that has never been taken off dry run has never moved anything, which is
the state every policy starts in and the most important thing on this row.

url.description: A short-lived delivery URL. Fetch it promptly; the token, not this URL, is what the recipient keeps.

PortalItem.description:
One asset in a pickup — or in a portal (Q.14), which shows the same facts for the same reasons.

`Deserialize` and `PartialEq` as well, because it now travels inside another response type: a portal page is
a list of these plus its branding, and one item shape means a client renders a pickup and a portal with the
same component.

preview_url.description: A short-lived, rights-checked preview URL, or nothing with a reason.

logo_url.description:
A preview URL for the logo, minted like any other: a logo is an asset, and an asset is delivered through
the chokepoint even when it is decoration.

query.description: What the visitor searched for, echoed so the page can show it.

total.description: How many assets the set holds after the search, which is not `items.len()` when the page is capped.

PortalRequest.description:
What a recipient sends. POST rather than GET even for the first look, so the passcode travels in a body —
a passcode in a query string is a passcode in every proxy log on the path.

PortalSetView.description:
What the portal shows for an order pickup (Q.13d).

A *set*, which the portal could not render before: `kind = 'order'` points at an order rather than one asset,
and until now that answered "this link shares something this portal cannot show yet".

Per-item previews and per-item refusals, deliberately. An order of forty photographs where two are unlicensed
is a pickup of thirty-eight, and collapsing that into one refusal would deny the recipient everything they were
entitled to because of somebody else's paperwork.

purpose.description: Why it was asked for. The recipient is usually the reason it was asked for.

reference.description: The order's human-quotable reference, so a recipient can say which pickup they mean.

preview_unavailable.description: Why there is no preview, when there is a stateable reason.

preview_url.description:
A short-lived delivery URL for the web rendition — a full rights-checked distribution, `None` when
rights refuse or no rendition exists yet. The share existing does not entitle anyone to pixels.

position.description:
Clamped rather than refused when out of range — a drag-and-drop that reports "position 47 of 12" is a
UI bug the user cannot act on, and the intent was clearly "the end".

recipients.description: Who to route it to. Required when `visibility` is `private`.

visibility.description: Defaults to public. Private is the deliberate choice, so it is the one you have to name.

PresentRequest.description: Changes to how a portal looks and reads.

ProfileRow.description: A profile as a client sees it.

defaults.description: Metadata applied to everything arriving under this profile, filling only what the upload omits.

metadata_type_id.description: The form uploads under this profile get. `None` lets the file's media class decide.

require_complete.description:
Whether the uploader should insist on required fields before proceeding.

A rule for the client, not a server-side gate: by the time an upload finalises its bytes are staged, and
refusing then would strand them over metadata a person could have supplied.

ProvenanceState.description:
Content-credential verification outcome. Mirrors the `assets.provenance_state` CHECK.

Four states rather than a boolean because they call for different responses: `None` is a file that
never had a credential, `Invalid` is one whose credential no longer matches its bytes, and
`Untrusted` is an intact credential from a signer outside any trust list. Collapsing them loses
the distinction between "no claim was made" and "a claim was made and broken".

QueryProblem.description:
Where a query was refused, so a UI can point at the character.

`Deserialize` as well as `Serialize` because it travels *inside* another response now — a translated
question reports the parser's own refusal rather than inventing a second vocabulary for the same failure.

at.description:
One-based column the parser stopped at, when it has one. A filter rail underlines from here; without it
a user gets "invalid query" and no idea which word.

code.description:
A stable machine-readable code, when the parser gave one. A UI maps it to a message in the user's
language, which prose cannot be.

suggestion.description:
The name the parser thinks was meant, when one is close enough (Q.17).

A suggestion beside a refusal, not a correction of it: the query still failed. The client offers it as
a one-click fix, which is the difference between "no field named `brnad`" and a search somebody can
finish.

available.description: False when the storage class does not offer this tier.

est_cost_cents.description:
Whole cents, rounded up. Zero when the pool has no prices recorded, which means "this deployment does
not know" rather than "free" — the screen should say so rather than promising nothing.

needs_approval.description: Whether choosing this would wait for an administrator instead of starting.

QuoteView.description: What restoring one asset would cost, per tier.

RailEntry.description: One thing the refine-search rail can show, and whether it does (Q.19).

entry.description:
`field:<key>`, `taxonomy:<uuid>` or `builtin:<name>` — the kind and the name, because a vocabulary
called `brand` and a field called `brand` are different entries.

kind.description: `field`, `taxonomy` or `builtin`, so a screen can group them.

label.description: What to show an administrator. A field's own label, a vocabulary's, or the built-in's name.

RailRequest.description: The ordered list of entries the rail should offer.

enabled.description:
Enabled entries, in the order they should appear. Anything the rail could show and this list omits is
recorded as *disabled* rather than forgotten — see `dam_db::rail::replace`.

stars.description: 1 to 5. There is no zero — clearing a rating is `DELETE`, because "no opinion" is not a low score.

assets_with_values.description:
How many assets still carry a value under this key. The values are **kept** — see `dam_db`'s
`fields::remove` — so this is what has gone invisible, not what was destroyed.

ReplaceKeyRequest.description: A replacement key for an existing credential.

RestoreOptions.description:
What a caller asks for.

Query parameters rather than a body, and not only for tidiness. A restore has no entity to send — the
asset is in the path and these two are modifiers — and an empty body under a JSON content-type is an
extractor rejection, which axum returns *before* the handler runs. That turned `POST .../restore` with no
body from a reader into a `400` about the body instead of the `403` the permission check owes them: the
gate never ran. A request with nothing to send should not have to send `{}` to find out it was refused.

keep_warm_days.description: How long the copy stays warm. Defaults to seven days (§6.5).

tier.description:
`expedited`, `standard` or `bulk`. Defaults to Standard — the middle, because a default of Expedited
spends ten times more than most callers meant to and a default of Bulk makes the feature feel broken.

RestoreState.description: Where a restore has got to, matching `object_placements.restore_state`.

RestoreTier.description: Retrieval speed for a restore, matching `restore_requests.tier`.

RestoreView.description: A restore, as the caller sees it.

est_cost_cents.description: What this is expected to cost, in whole cents, rounded up so an approved estimate is not exceeded.

eta_at.description: When the copy is expected. The slow end of the documented window, so an ETA met early beats one missed.

expires_at.description:
When the temporary copy lapses. The storage class never changed, so after this the asset needs
restoring again.

joined_existing.description:
True when this request was already in flight and the caller has joined it rather than starting a
second one. Two people asking for the same archived asset share one retrieval and one charge.

ReviewRow.description: One asset in the review queue.

RightsState.description: Rights evaluation outcome for an asset. Mirrors the `assets.rights_state` CHECK.

policies_in_dry_run.description:
Restated on the response, because "I pressed run and nothing moved" is otherwise a support ticket
rather than a policy that is still in dry run.

SchemaField.description: A field definition with the numbers an administrator needs before touching it.

assets_with_values.description:
How many live assets carry a value under this key.

The number that decides whether an edit is safe, so it is on the row rather than behind another
request: an administrator deciding whether to remove a field should not have to go and ask.

SetAssetTypeRequest.description: What to set an asset's type to. `null` clears it, which is different from omitting the member.

ShareRequest.description: What a client asks for when sharing an asset.

allow_original.description: Whether the recipient may fetch the original, rather than only the web rendition.

expires_in_hours.description: Hours until the link stops working. Absent means no expiry — revocation is then the only way it ends.

passcode.description: Plaintext; hashed with argon2id server-side and never stored or returned.

ShareRow.description: One row in the management list.

live.description: Whether the link still works, so the list does not make a reader re-derive it from four columns.

SkipView.description: One object a run would leave alone.

detail.description:
The human sentence, where there is more to say — a pin's reason, or the date something becomes
eligible.

reason.description: A stable machine-readable reason, for grouping a plan of ten thousand into a handful of lines.

SortOrder.description:
The orders a client may ask for.

A closed set on the wire as well as in SQL. Accepting a column name would make the ORDER BY
caller-supplied, and validating one against a list is the same list written twice.

Spotlight.description: A saved search, as a dashboard tile.

cached_count.description:
The stored count, and named as stored: it is a cached number a worker refreshes, never an access decision
and never this caller's count. A tile that presented it as "your results" would be lying to a scoped
reader.

mine.description: Whether this caller owns it, so a tile can say "yours" rather than implying everyone's is.

SuggestedTagView.description: A tag waiting for a decision.

confidence.description: As the model claimed. Shown so a reviewer can sort, never as a reason to skip reviewing.

votes.description: How many generators proposed it independently.

Suggestion.description: What somebody is probably about to type (Q.17).

count.description: How many visible assets carry it. The list is ordered by this within each source.

fragment.description:
The query fragment to insert. The client's job is to put a string in a box; a suggestion it had to
assemble would be a second place where the query language is spoken and can be got wrong.

source.description: `field`, `term` or `filename` — what the client groups by.

within.description: The field key or taxonomy label it came from. Absent for a filename.

TagDecision.description: A decision about a suggested tag.

accept.description: `true` confirms the tag, `false` rejects it. Both are recorded: the rejections are the training signal.

TransitionView.description: One object a run would move.

min_duration_until.description: When this object could next move, after this one. The minimum billable duration the new class starts.

UsageOptions.description: What a person may declare a download as.

channels.description: Channels any of this tenant's licences reference, inclusions and exclusions alike.

default_channel.description:
What a download is recorded as when nobody declares anything, so a client can show it as the default
rather than inventing its own.

declared.description: Whether somebody stated this use, or the API defaulted it. The difference is the whole point of asking.

oneOf.description: Who took it. Absent for a download by a machine credential, which has no person behind it.

ValidationProblem.description: Why an edit was refused, field by field.

code.description:
A stable machine-readable code. Stable because a client branches on it and a UI maps it to a message
in the user's language, neither of which can be done with prose.

key.description: The payload key, or the field key for a missing required field.

VerifyResult.description: What a verification call found out.

detail.description: What the provider said, or what went wrong, in one sentence somebody can act on.

model.description: The model that actually answered, which is not always the one asked for.

worth_retrying.description: Whether trying again might help. A rejected key never will; a throttle will.

is_current.description: Whether this is the version listings and downloads resolve to.

q.description: A term to narrow the set by. Ignored when the portal does not allow searching.

Worklist.description: How many assets are in no category, and some of them.

sample.description: The first few, so a client can link straight into them.

total.description: Every uncategorised asset this caller can see.

WorklistView.description: One worklist, and how much of it there is for this caller.

count.description: How many assets *this caller* can see on it.

explanation.description:
What being on this list means, and what to do about it. Sent from the server rather than written into
the client, so the sentence and the SQL that decides it live in the same place.

key.description: The stable name, used in the URL.

label.description: What to call it on screen.

urgent.description:
Whether the list is worth leading with when it is not empty.

Two of these are exposure rather than tidiness — an asset served past its expiry date, and a licence
about to lapse — and a screen that sorted by count would bury them under a thousand missing captions.
